meta.title: Who really said "Anything that is too stupid to be spoken is sung"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Voltaire. The line is a paraphrase of Beaumarchais’ Figaro in The Barber of Seville (1775) — and Shaw’s Man and Superman jokes about the mix-up.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Anything that is too stupid to be spoken is sung'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Voltaire. It paraphrases Beaumarchais’ Figaro in The Barber of Seville (1775); Shaw’s Man and Superman even stages the misattribution.

answer.label: Not Voltaire — actually Beaumarchais
answer.authorDates: 1732–1799 · French playwright, author of the Figaro comedies
answer.sourceLine: The quotable line belongs to Beaumarchais, not Voltaire. In Le Barbier de Séville (1775), Act I, sc. ii, Figaro quips “Aujourd’hui, ce qui ne vaut pas la peine d’être dit, on le chante” — “nowadays, what isn’t worth saying is sung.” The familiar English “anything too stupid to be spoken is sung” is a loose paraphrase; George Bernard Shaw’s Man and Superman (1903) even dramatises the mix-up, having a character credit “Voltaire” before being corrected to Beaumarchais.

source.excerpt: Aujourd’hui, ce qui ne vaut pas la peine d’être dit, on le chante. — “Nowadays, what isn’t worth saying is sung.”
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under Voltaire’s Misattributed section and gives the true source as Beaumarchais, Le Barbier de Séville (1775), Act I, sc. ii.
The original words are Figaro’s: “Aujourd’hui, ce qui ne vaut pas la peine d’être dit, on le chante” — “what isn’t worth saying is sung.”
Shaw baked the mix-up into Man and Superman (1903): Tanner credits “Voltaire”; Straker corrects him to “Bow Mar Shay,” i.e. Beaumarchais.
The Voltaire Foundation (OUP) discusses how one-liners drift onto Voltaire and quotes Shaw’s scene crediting “Voltaire” before correcting it to Beaumarchais — the memorable line is Beaumarchais’.
source.excerptNote: Spoken by Figaro in Le Barbier de Séville, Act I, sc. ii. The popular English “anything too stupid to be spoken is sung” is a paraphrase of this line, not a quotation of Voltaire.
source.rightsNote: The source work, Beaumarchais’ Le Barbier de Séville, was first performed and published in 1775 and is long in the public domain; the English paraphrase circulated by Shaw’s Man and Superman (1903) is likewise public domain in the United States. The exact English wording “too stupid to be spoken is sung” is an anonymous later paraphrase with no identifiable copyright holder.

author.name: Pierre-Augustin Caron de Beaumarchais
author.heading: About Pierre-Augustin Caron de Beaumarchais
author.metaLine: 1732–1799 · French playwright & author of the Figaro comedies
author.bio: Pierre-Augustin Caron de Beaumarchais (1732–1799) was a French playwright, watchmaker, inventor and financier best remembered for the two Figaro comedies — Le Barbier de Séville (1775) and Le Mariage de Figaro (1784), later set to music by Rossini and Mozart. The quip about singing what isn’t worth saying is spoken by his fast-talking valet Figaro in the first play’s opening act.

misattribution.heading: Why it’s pinned on Voltaire
misattribution.intro: Voltaire is the internet’s favourite magnet for stray Enlightenment wit, so a snappy anti-opera one-liner drifts to him by default — but the quotable line is Beaumarchais’, and the mix-up is over a century old.

items.why: Wikiquote files it under Voltaire’s ‘Misattributed’ section, pointing instead to Beaumarchais’ Le Barbier de Séville (1775). The Voltaire Foundation likewise treats it as a misattribution, quoting Shaw’s scene that corrects “Voltaire” to Beaumarchais — not that Voltaire wrote this line.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Figaro’s in Beaumarchais’ Barber of Seville; the English “too stupid to be spoken is sung” is a paraphrase that Shaw’s Man and Superman already joked was wrongly given to Voltaire.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The barb is aimed at opera: a sentiment too silly to survive being merely spoken can still pass if you set it to music. Figaro tosses it off in the opening scene of Le Barbier de Séville as a piece of worldly cynicism.
By 1903 the attribution was already a running joke: in Shaw’s Man and Superman, Tanner credits “Voltaire” and his chauffeur Straker corrects him — “It wasn’t Voltaire: it was Bow Mar Shay.”
context.pull: “Nowadays, what isn’t worth saying is sung.”
